record.title: Self-Credit uses cross-rollout turn citations to assign credit in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning
record.summary: The arXiv preprint introduces Self-Credit, a long-horizon agentic RL method that has a policy cite earlier turns in its own summaries, then adjusts turn-level credit by comparing cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for each prompt. Across three-seed evaluations, the authors report higher accuracy than the strongest tested agentic-RL baselines on BrowseComp-Plus with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, and on GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch with Gemma4-E4B. Evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge scoring; independent reproduction and end-to-end compute comparison are not established.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The v1 preprint describes Self-Credit, which asks the agent to cite earlier turns in its generated summaries and then rescales cited-turn credit across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt before reweighting turn-level advantages.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On BrowseComp-Plus, the authors report three-seed Pass@1 of 47.0% for Qwen3-32B and 40.6% for Qwen3-8B, respectively 5.6 and 8.5 percentage points above the strongest reported baseline in each setting. For Gemma4-E4B, they report 39.2% on text-only GAIA and 16.7% on xBench-DeepSearch, 4.9 and 4.7 points above the strongest reported baselines. These are paper-reported results, not independently reproduced.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s BrowseComp-Plus ablations, removing intra-group rescaling, repeated-failure penalties or self-generated citations lowered the reported accuracy; the size of the drop varied across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B. This supports component sensitivity within the authors’ setup, not an independently established causal effect.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction was found or performed; benchmark accuracy uses LLM-as-judge.
The paper does not establish whether gains persist under matched end-to-end compute or across other model families and task environments.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported gains generalize, a self-generated credit signal that uses both successful and failed rollouts could change how sparse outcome rewards train multi-step research agents. Its present consequence is meaningful within agent post-training, but evidence is limited to one preprint and tested models/tasks.
limitations: All performance values are author-reported in one arXiv preprint; no independent reproduction was performed.

Accuracy is adjudicated by LLM-as-judge: a separate Qwen3-32B judge on BrowseComp-Plus and rubric-based LLM judging for deep-research tasks. Sensitivity to alternate blinded judges or human assessment is unknown.
BrowseComp-Plus training and evaluation use a static corpus and search index; deep-research evaluation uses an open web search API, so conditions differ across datasets.
The experiments cover Qwen3-8B/32B and Gemma4-E4B on specified search/deep-research tasks; transfer to other model families, agent tasks or production reliability is not established.
Independent artifacts and full end-to-end compute/cost comparisons were not verified.

The method assumes that turns contribute independently to outcomes, although the authors note that later actions can depend on earlier retrieved evidence; this approximation may distort turn-level credit.

relationships.summary: Both address agentic post-training for long-horizon tasks: R2S modifies the teacher’s token-level scoring signal before OPD, while Self-Credit derives turn-level advantage weights from the policy’s citations and outcomes across rollouts.
Both contribute to the research desk’s evidence base on agentic post-training and how feedback granularity shapes learned behavior.

brief.summary: The arXiv preprint introduces Self-Credit, a long-horizon agentic RL method that has a policy cite earlier turns in its own summaries, then adjusts turn-level credit by comparing cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for each prompt. Across three-seed evaluations, the authors report higher accuracy than the strongest tested agentic-RL baselines on BrowseComp-Plus with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, and on GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch with Gemma4-E4B. Evaluation relies on LLM-as-judge scoring; independent reproduction and end-to-end compute comparison are not established.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report three-seed BrowseComp-Plus test accuracy of 47.0% for Qwen3-32B and 40.6% for Qwen3-8B, compared with the strongest reported baselines of 41.4% and 32.1%. With Gemma4-E4B, they report 39.2% on GAIA versus 34.3% and 16.7% on xBench-DeepSearch versus 12.0%. Scoring is author-reported and uses LLM judges.
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors state that all compared methods share the major training configuration and are run on an NVIDIA B200 GPU cluster, but the paper does not provide an end-to-end resource ledger for the extra citation-bearing summary generation and related overhead. Therefore no total compute or cost advantage is established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv v1 paper and its described experiments are publicly accessible. the research desk inspected the paper text and did not execute code or reproduce the results. No code/data release was established in this review.
technical.mechanism: When context compaction occurs, the policy summarizes interaction history and cites turns it considers important. For each prompt, intra-group rescaling compares cited turns across successful and failed rollouts: repeated turns shared with failures lose credit, success-specific turns gain credit, and failure-specific turns receive stronger negative credit. The resulting weights reweight turn-level advantages in group-based policy optimization.
technical.regime: BrowseComp-Plus: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, with 747 training examples and 83 test examples using a static corpus/index. Deep research: Gemma4-E4B trained on 1,000 OpenResearcher QA pairs; evaluation on text-only GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch. The paper reports three seeds.
technical.reproducibility: Three-seed results are reported. Independent reproduction, public code/data status, judge robustness and exact training-compute accounting were not verified. Appendix B also states that an invalid or empty citation line can cause the whole rollout to receive zero reward, and that turn-credit matching assumes independence between turns despite sequential evidence dependencies.
technical.strongest_baseline: The authors compare against GRPO, GiGPO, SUPO and ECHO. ECHO is the strongest reported baseline for the cited benchmark comparisons. Cross-paper or independently harmonized benchmark parity was not established.

brief.title: Self-Credit uses cross-rollout turn citations to assign credit in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning
brief.why_it_matters: If the paper’s results generalize, self-generated evidence citations combined with cross-rollout credit rescaling could improve post-training for multi-step search and research agents without adding a separate learned critic. The evidence is one preprint on a bounded benchmark and model set, with judge-based evaluation and no independent reproduction.

related.summary: Both address agentic post-training for long-horizon tasks: R2S modifies the teacher’s token-level scoring signal before OPD, while Self-Credit derives turn-level advantage weights from the policy’s citations and outcomes across rollouts.

other.title: A reward-free teacher repair improves agentic on-policy distillation on three text-agent benchmarks
other.summary: Zhao and Yu introduce Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which uses selected teacher takeovers from high-disagreement states of an untrained student to fine-tune the teacher’s token-level scorer before ordinary on-policy distillation (OPD). The student still trains against the frozen scorer with the standard sampled reverse-KL objective; task reward is not used to train it. Across ALFWorld, WebShop and ScienceWorld, the authors report that R2S outperformed three recent agentic-OPD baselines in all twelve model/student/environment cells, averaging 12.8 success points above the strongest baseline in each cell; Appendix E reports that R2S exceeds every baseline in mean on all 24 evaluation splits. The study uses two Qwen teacher families and four students. These are preprint-author results, not independently reproduced; the main table uses one training run per cell and the repair requires up to 19,200 teacher takeover episodes.

related.summary: Both contribute to the research desk’s evidence base on agentic post-training and how feedback granularity shapes learned behavior.

other.title: A paper reports semantic stop-token alignment reduces length inflation in on-policy distillation
other.summary: A September 17 preprint studies length inflation in sampled-token on-policy distillation (OPD). It argues that when a base student and post-trained teacher encode the same stopping decision with different tokens, the teacher can give a negative signal to the student’s sampled EOS while the teacher-preferred token receives little support. Across Qwen3, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3, the authors report that aligning total probability over semantically equivalent stop tokens in the distillation signal reduces mismatch-driven length and clipping; merely expanding the decoder stop set does not. An earlier OPD paper already describes EOS canonicalization in Appendix D, so the basic alignment idea is prior art; the newer paper adds cross-family empirical comparisons, a shared-declared-set Gemma test and stage-wise residual analysis. It also reports late-stage K2-Horizon re-inflation after correction. These are author-run, single-turn mathematical-reasoning results; multi-turn/tool semantics and independent replication remain open.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
